utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've temporarily forgotten and failed to mark which paragraph I was at. My mistake. If I can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While counsel is looking for the paragraph, Mr. Tanic, could you try and keep your answers as narrowly focused as possible. You've got a lot of evidence to give and it's important that we hear it, but our time is limited, and we'll get through it more quickly and you can get away more quickly if you would just focus on the questions and answer them. If counsel wants more information, he can always ask for it. If you'd keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best to respect those guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it was paragraph 53, was it? I may be wrong about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Kwon reminds me the private chain of command was the last topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. It was paragraph 54 and indeed I now have found the mark I've left myself. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you were telling us yesterday of the fact-finding mission and of the recommendations that it was able to make. Were those recommendations - yes or no - acted on by the accused?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he ever pronounce the KLA to be a terrorist organisation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the legal framework, but just as a political accusation. But not within the law as provided for by the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes/no will do to this answer: Did he ever proclaim a state of emergency in Kosovo which would have allowed for official action against terrorists?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in keeping with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just yes or no to this, and I mean just yes or no: Following the recommendations of the fact-finding group, were you aware of the accused laying blame for what was happening in Kosovo elsewhere? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From whom did you hear this account of blame, if not from the accused himself? From whom did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the leadership of the State Security Service and from political structures with whom we had a regular exchange of information, both in parliament and in the government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in a sentence, what was now being said by the leadership as to who bore responsibility for the problems in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it turned out at the end that the responsibility for the problems in Kosovo was to be borne by a group of unresponsible -- irresponsible policemen, and the Security Service and the army that were covering up the facts and did not wish to act against the terrorists. Those were the rumours and story bandied about within the circle, inner circles of Yugoslav and Serbian parent authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me a minute. Mr. Tanic, you just mentioned that the action against the KLA was not done in legal framework. Is it right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you clarify more about the legal framework? Does it mean that the actions taken in the Kosovo area was kind of unofficial one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't say they were unofficial. All I can say is that they were illegal with respect to our constitution and legal frameworks, at least as far as I am aware of them, and as I was able to check up in consultations. So an extraordinary state of affairs or an emergency situation is proclaimed by the Assembly of Yugoslavia. That is provided for by the constitution. It is the Assembly that decides on war and peace. And to proclaim a group terrorist, you have to follow a procedure that is much stricter than a political qualification by saying that somebody is a terrorist or is not. So the actions were official, but they weren't in conformity and dovetailed to the constitution and the legal provisions of the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's one event that occurred rather later, on which you draw a particular inference. It's paragraph 55. And I want you to deal with this very shortly. Was there, on the 23rd of March of 1999, a session of the Republic of the Serbian Assembly which was televised, in the course of which Mr. Milutinovic made an observation? If yes, just tell us about the observation and, in one sentence, its significance.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the Serbian Assembly meeting held on the 23rd of March, 1999, first of all there was a completely illegal discussion as to whether Yugoslavia would enter into a war with the NATO pact or not, and that does not come under the competencies of the Assembly of Serbia but the Assembly of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, we're going to get on better if you remember what His Honour Judge May said to you this morning and if you listen carefully to my questions. We'll do this as an experiment to make sure that we get it right. What I asked you is this: On that 23rd of March, did Mr. Milutinovic make an observation? And, if yes, tell us about the observation and, in one sentence, its significance. So all I want from you is two things: what he said and what was important about it.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milutinovic said that the political problem with the Kosovar Albanians did not exist at all, neither did it exist in Rambouillet, the problem of a political agreement, and that the Western powers and the Contact Group was -- offered the Serbian delegation in Rambouillet a political agreement of whatever kind it liked, as it saw fit and as it understood the interests of Serbia and Belgrade and Yugoslavia, but that the only problem in that was that the Contact Group and the international community wished to ensure the implementation of that political agreement with the ground troops who would be present in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And so the significance of that observation, in your understanding, is what?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The significance of that observation, in my opinion, is that that talk about the fact that the Western forces and the Contact Group wanted to impose a bad political agreement for Serbia and Yugoslavia at the detriment of Serbia was completely incorrect, not to say untruthful, because Mr. Milutinovic did acknowledge that we could have had a favourable agreement, favourable to Serbia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 57. In the course of that Serbian Assembly session, did other SBS representatives make statements contrary to or in support of war?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they spoke in favour of a war conflict, but in complete contrast to what Milutinovic had said. He said that we were being offered a bad political agreement and that that is why we had to accept war, to go to war with NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, paragraph 58. Did Mr. Vuk Draskovic provide an alternative?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes, he did, on behalf of a group of people who compiled an alternative solution to the Serbian Assembly which should have been sufficient to avoid this conflict with the NATO pact, which would have been suicidal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now, then, please, look at a document which comes in three parts. It needs a little explanation. And can we have TX 8, please. The original, Your Honours, is an old-style fax paper. The significance will become obvious, but includes that, of course, old-style fax paper used to degrade over time, so it was recopied when it came into the possession of the OTP. But I think we can probably survive on this version. Now, if we'd like to lay the original on the overhead projector so that we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, is this a document that you've seen before and indeed that you received?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What's on the overhead projector on the moment is, I think, an original fax document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dated March 24th, 1999. How did you receive it, please?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is draft conclusions, as you can see, and it was sent to the deputy group --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now let's put the -- we'll move --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for a meeting of the Assembly that we mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now please lay the English translation on the overhead projector. Then we'll come back to the original in a minute. And if we look at the draft conclusions, running through them: 1. At its session on the 23rd of March, the National Assembly accepted positions and work of the Republic of Serbia state delegation at Rambouillet and Paris. 2. The National Assembly affirms that the state delegation made every effort and did everything it could, in direct dialogue with the delegation from the separatist movement of Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija, both in Rambouillet and Paris, et cetera. 3. It is with regret that the National Assembly notes that the international goodwill mediators and co-chairs of the talks in Rambouillet and Paris did not find a way to persuade the delegation of the separatist movement to sit at the same table. 4. And there's an illegible line ... be ascribed to the state delegation of Serbia, which insisted the whole time on direct discussion. Instead the blame lies exclusively with the delegation of the separatist and terrorist movement. 5. And I'm summarising it to save time: The National Assembly appeals to eminent representatives of the Contact Group to find a way to get the delegation of the Albanian separatist movement to sit at the same negotiating table. 6. If the delegation of the Albanian separatist movement does not want to talk and reach such an agreement, then the state delegation is prepared, at any time, and so on. 7. As soon as any political agreement is reached, the state delegation of Serbia and the Federal Republic is prepared to conclude an agreement. 8. The National Assembly demands an end to all threats of aggression by the NATO pact. 9. Expresses the determination of Serbia to reach a quick, peaceful, and just agreement. Now, if we go back to the -- well, let's just read 7 in detail. Again, 7: "As soon as any political agreement is reached, the state delegation of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is prepared to conclude an agreement with the international community on the application of the said political agreement, with a clearly specified and strictly limited mandate from the UN Security Council." Now, let's go to the original, please, the fax copy, on the second sheet, where we can see that there is a handwritten addition there. Just yes or no: Did somebody tell you whose hand that was in?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who told you whose hand it was in?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got that information from Vuk Draskovic and Dusan Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And whose handwriting did they say that was?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to that information, it is the handwriting of Mr. Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you seen his handwriting yourself before? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on two or three occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Let's now go back to the English version to see what the amendment reads. And so at the end of paragraph 7, the amendment in hand reads: "Respecting the sovereignty of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. May that be given an exhibit number, then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked Prosecution's Exhibit 149.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, did the witness answer to your question how he got this document? He said it was sent to the deputies. Was it the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the only answer he gave, and it wasn't sufficient. I'll get a little bit more -- I'm sorry not to have dealt with that properly earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You heard His Honour Judge Kwon's question. It was sent to the deputies. How did you receive it yourself? How come you were talking to Vuk Draskovic about it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got the document from my own personal archive and from my own knowledge, from the president of our deputy group, and I noticed differences between what had been agreed and what was actually discussed at the meeting. So I wanted to have the paper, to have the document, to see whether it had been circulated, and that's how had I came by that paper, or rather, the draft conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how did you come to be talking to Mr. Draskovic about it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only with him, but with a series of other individuals. Well, for the simple reason that I was included in the group of people who prepared a document which would have been sufficient to avoid this unnecessary and suicidal war with the NATO pact, and I received information that Mr. Milosevic, in principle, was in agreement but that all that had to be done was to find a solution which would not be to the detriment of the sovereignty of Serbia and Yugoslavia. And at the Assembly meeting of Serbia, I saw a completely different discussion taking place which was directly leading into an unnecessary war with NATO. And this enormous difference cropped up over two days, and I think that that caused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That again is the point that I had in mind. Just stick, if you would, to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just so that we understand the position, Mr. Tanic: The draft conclusions, apart from the handwritten addition, are they conclusions that you accept had been reached and were a plan that had been made?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, yes, between Mr. Draskovic and Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what you're saying, but correct me if I've got it wrong, but what you're saying is that this plan, even with its handwritten amendment, was inconsistent with the debate you heard in the Assembly where Milutinovic and others were speaking; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because capital differences rose to the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think there was -- I needn't trouble with that. We'll move on to the next page, paragraph 65. From your knowledge, Mr. Tanic, going back a couple of years, 1996, 1997, how large or small was the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to professional intelligence on the security assessment, about 2.000 people who were poorly armed and distributed in small groups, generally young villagers, young male villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The KLA leadership was where, and how numerous was it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the true leadership was, for the most part, abroad, perhaps not more than five or ten people: Switzerland, Germany, Croatia, from time to time Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday there were already indications from other countries that they would give assistance to Serbia if it was determined to control the KLA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions for the political -- based on the conditions of the political solution for Kosovo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what, if anything, had President Rugova said was his intention so far as KLA or other radicals were concerned? What was he prepared to do for them?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, they waged a policy of non-violent resistance and they were ready to politically marginalise the KLA if a political solution to Kosovo were to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 67 to 72 I can deal with in, I think, one sentence. As to the possibility of foreign troops functioning on the soil of Serbia, was there any, to your knowledge, constitutional objection to that happening?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 74. In the late 1990s, but maybe earlier, but certainly in the late 1990s, were there occasions of Kosovar Albanians being killed in the course of this developing conflict?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, already at the beginning of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were these deaths discussed in the political circles in which you moved? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this topic brought to the attention of the accused? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I'm getting the English interpretation on my headsets -- the French, sorry. I'm getting the French.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this topic brought to the attention of the accused? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And again, do you know - yes or no - what his reaction was from time to time to the problem of Kosovar Albanians being killed? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, did you learn of that from direct contact with the accused or from other sources, or perhaps from both?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From both. First of all, from other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then also from the accused himself?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the occasion that I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When he said what about the deaths of Kosovar Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that there was collective support of the Albanian people to the Albanian terrorists, and so if there was collective support, then the death of civilians is something that will come about in a war conflict as an unfortunate consequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I appreciate your attempt to be concise, but it's not clear to me how it is being alleged that these Kosovar Albanians met their death.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, Mr. Tanic: The deaths of which we're speaking, how did they come about, typically?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they came about -- and I have to explain this at length. I find it difficult to strike a balance between being precise and being allowed to explain, so may I get instructions as to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the reason why I'm asking is that this is in the early stages of the conflict, the developing conflict, and I consider it useful, in fact necessary, to find out exactly how it is alleged that these Kosovar Albanians met their death. And you can give the answer as concisely as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those deaths came about through the regular activities of our police force against the Albanian terrorists. However, bearing in mind the fact that this activity was conducted in the manner that I described previously, according to the chain of semi-personal command, without constitutional and legal frameworks, without police logistics and security logistics, what happened was that, together with the terrorists, civilians would be killed too, and a large number of civilians at that, sometimes larger, sometimes smaller. The classical example took place in the Donje Prekaze village in March 1998. If you want me to, I can explain that case to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This would be in 1997, or what year was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1998, the beginning of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you could give us some concrete conversation between you and Milosevic at that time, in concrete terms, your comment and Mr. Milosevic's answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yesterday that it wasn't a conversation in the classical sense, but a sort of short verbal communication. When it was said by Mr. Milosevic that the Albanians had the massive support of the people and that it was a case of mass terrorism in fact. So this wasn't, in fact, a conversation, and I was quite specific when I described it yesterday. Because you couldn't discuss those matters with Mr. Milosevic, at least I couldn't, because I didn't have that rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as you were aware, were other senior -- were senior officials at that time, including Perisic, Stanisic, Mihajlovic and others, were they taking any line on the death of Kosovar Albanians, either a line that was consistent with the attitude of the accused, as you've described it, or different? What was the position?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of that much better, because I could discuss these matters with these persons at much greater length at meetings. Their positions were mostly to the contrary to the position held by the accused. They were opposed to the unselective use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: More recently, and I think probably in the course of the preparation of the book you've told us about, you've had conversations with various people, including with Perisic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of those conversations, were you shown a letter, which we'll have a look at, dated the 23rd of July of 1998, from Perisic to the accused? Is this the letter that you were shown by Mr. Perisic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the original can just be -- or not the original. If the B/C/S version could be laid on the overhead projector, first of all as to the first page, so the accused can see what it is. The next sheet, please. The date, the 23rd of July of 1998, and we can see the address to the president. And then if we just look on to the last page, we can see the signature of Momcilo Perisic. So if we can now put the English version on the overhead projector, please, starting at the first substantive page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we do, we need to know where this comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this -- first of all, do you recognise this as the letter that you were shown?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the letter of the Chief of General Staff, addressed to Mr. Milosevic, as President of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In fact, this version comes, I think, from a book, is that correct, the letter having been published?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's quite clear to me. But it is quite identical to the original of the letter that I saw, read, studied, and discussed with several people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It comes from a book, the witness's book, is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. It's another book, and I think it's -- the front cover of it, I think, gives you -- in the original. And it's got the authors at the top and the date of publication at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I have the whole book here. If the Court wants it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I just want to know how it comes to be in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I hope the method of summarising these texts for people who can probably read faster than I can read out loud is satisfactory, to save time. The English translation, by the way, of the book title is "Fire and Flood." I'm grateful to Ms. Graham. She had already told me that, and I should have told you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Dear Mr. President: Having analysed your attitude towards the Yugoslav army, I need to urgently convey to you certain facts ..." Paragraph 2: "I hope you've had an opportunity to assure yourself of the high military patriotic consciousness..." and et cetera. Paragraph 3: "We would not be correct and sincere under these fateful circumstances if, as professionals who safeguarded the VJ and the SRJ in conditions known to you, we did not point out the following negative facts: The constant tendency to use the VJ outside the system's institutions; the separation of VJ units from the Yugoslav army; the attempt by unauthorised persons to command VJ units, passing over command levels in official conversations with VJ members; conducting personnel policy on an unlawful basis and without criteria; financial expenditures outside the law" and so on. Then it gives some typical examples: "The tendency to use the army outside the system's institutions." It says that the state -- The situation in Kosovo and Metohija could have been overcome if a state of emergency had been declared when written proposals had been sent, which had not been accepted. And over the page to B, setting out a request to the government to ensure legal definitions, the proclamation of one of the following: A state of emergency and material and financial conditions. Then it goes on to say: Using the VJ in this manner is untenable for three reasons: The army is not being used adequately and the effects are minor; true goals not being achieved; and we are being accused of behaving as traitors. The use of the army in this manner has been noticed by observers which may provoke reprisals from the international community and NATO. The proposed solution was to use the VJ lawfully and, "The position is clear to us," this part concludes, "but we must have a legal political decision." And 2: "Separation of units from the VJ. You have decided to separate the Guards Brigade from the VJ," and the suggestion in the letter is that that's not lawful and that the decision should be annulled. Attempts by -- 3, attempts by unauthorised persons to command VJ units. Then this: "Constant aspirations by members of the MUP to have some VJ units subordinated to them leads to misunderstandings if the units are not given, and if they are given, this represents unauthorised and unprofessional use which has counter-effects, the best examples being Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Decani and Orahovac." "B, attempt by civilian members of the staff to command the corps. The responsibility of the Corps Commander is to evaluate the situation, plan operations for the VJ and the MUP in cooperation with civilian members of the staff and the MUP, and report to Sainovic and Minic." And then it goes on to say: "In practice, the commander of the Pristina Corps plans what he is ordered to do, which is at the request of Sainovic, Minic and the MUP, and is then turned in to their service for planning and realisation. Since it is his wish, like the wish of us all, to realise the plan if others cannot or will not do it, he does it with the Pristina Corps units, which leads to illegal, unsystematic and inadequate use of VJ units, thus violating the system..." and so on. And the proposal for this part of the letter is to disallow command of the VJ outside the system of military subordination and unity of command and that the third army should set up a forward command post in Pristina. 4: Passing over command levels and official conversations with VJ members, the letter says: "According to VJ service regulations, you have the right to conduct official conversations with all members of the VJ, however you sometimes do this without the knowledge of the Chief of the General Staff, contrary to military subordination and unity of command. Violation of these principles leads to the break-up of the unity of the VJ. Proposal: Respect the principles of military subordination." 5: Conducting personnel policy on an unlawful basis and without criteria. Sets out: "Generals and colonels are often promoted at the VSO and outside VSO on an unlawful basis, without decrees or criteria, which has far-reaching negative effects in the VJ." VSO, please, Mr. Tanic? What does VSO stand for?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not on our list of acronyms, I don't think. It goes on to say: "Necessary to respect the laws, decrees, and criteria for promotion." Over the page in the English: "Each institution depends on the main elements of the system," and sets out what a general should be and proposes refraining promotion of colonels and generals to higher ranks if this is not in agreement with the law. And 6, financial expenditure outside the law. "You often order me to give up movable and immovable property for the needs of the MUP on the basis of the SRJ law on property. Neither do you have the right to order me nor do I have the right to carry out orders regarding material payments." The solution proposed: "Direct such requests to the legal owner of the property, namely, the government." Then various concluding paragraphs which we can read rapidly to ourselves, with the concern that if the proposals made aren't met, second to the last paragraph on the English version of that page,: "Otherwise, this sole highly functional Yugoslav institution will turn into a non-functional and disunited amorphous mass." The rest of it we can read. Just a couple of comments from you on what we've been looking at. Can you help us? We saw reference to the Guards Brigade. Can you help us with the significance of that, please, if any?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade was singled out to be under Mr. Slobodan Milosevic's personal command in order for them to carry out orders that the army would not have carried out because it would have implied illegal use of force.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you could speak a little more slowly, Mr. Tanic. I know you're getting a bombardment of instructions as to how you should give your evidence. A little more slowly, please. Bombardment from me. I'm not describing anybody else's addresses in those terms. Similarly, any significance in the reference to civilians giving instructions? Can you deal with that, the civilian staff?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that pertains to this private chain of command that went through the personal representatives and envoys of Mr. Slobodan Milosevic. These were civilians who were engaged in the staff for Kosovo, or rather, in the commission for Kosovo. The army cannot receive orders from civilian persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The exhibit in Serb, you said it's the original one. So is this the copy -- photocopy of the original letter or is it printed again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is a photocopy of the original letter, but probably adjusted for printing purposes, because it was written on A4 because that is the official format for official communications, A4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is it that Mr. Perisic kept this letter after he had sent this letter to Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course he kept a copy. That is official documentation. It can be seen from the letterhead and the number and also it says "confidential," and also the official channels through which it was sent. The Chief of General Staff has the right to retain a copy of such official documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he serve as chief of the staff of the army later on, after he sent this letter to the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for another three and a half to four months, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll be coming to the end of Perisic's engagement in due course. But I think it may be that what His Honour would like to know just a little more in detail is this:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When Perisic showed you a document, did he show you his own copy that he had retained or did he show you a copy that had already been published in somebody else's book?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not then. This copy was not printed in any book. He showed me his very own copy, two or three years before it had been published in any book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just to go back to the first typical example given, the chief of staff says that the situation in Kosovo and Metohija could have been overcome if a state of emergency had been declared, as indeed he had recommended. The witness is not a lawyer, but would he be able to say, briefly, how the declaration of a state of emergency would have made the difference? Does he have any knowledge of the powers that would be available to Mr. Milosevic in a state of emergency that would have been critical in that situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you've heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If he doesn't have that knowledge, then he need not answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've heard the question and its limitations. Can you help His Honour? You've touched on it to some degree, but can you help a little further?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that I can be of assistance, but it is up to the Trial Chamber to decide whether I'm capable of doing it or not. According to our constitution, Mr. Milosevic would not have any greater or lesser powers if a state of emergency had been declared in a regular way through the Assembly of Yugoslavia. The problem lies elsewhere. If a state of emergency had been declared by the Assembly of Yugoslavia, it would have had to be preceded by a serious national debate as to whether there was really terrorism in a part of the country to such an extent that it did necessitate the use of the army and the police, or was this not the case. So then we would have had an in-depth discussion as to whether the problem of terrorism in Kosovo was really so great or whether it was just blown out of all proportion, fabricated, whatever. On the other hand, the declaration of a state of emergency also makes it incumbent upon the president of the republic, in this case Mr. Milosevic, to take other political action, and this would have prevented the voluntaristic and non-selective use of force. This is the way I see it and this is the best I can do in terms of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions arising from the document we've been looking at. VJ equipment going to the MUP - just, again, yes or no to this question - do you know the involvement, if any, of the accused in the decision that VJ equipment should go to the MUP? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you learn that from the accused himself, from documents, or from being told about it by an individual?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the accused personally. I didn't find out from him directly. I found out from talking to the leaders of the SDB, politicians, and through my insight into certain documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, in those circumstances, can you tell us, please, what from those sources you understood to be the involvement, if any, of the accused in the movement of VJ equipment to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my understanding, the participation of the accused, Mr. Milosevic, was crucial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, but we may return to some of those topics when they become relevant in later passages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit 150.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this this book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this book becoming an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The letter, for the moment, is an exhibit. If you want the book -- just a moment. Let the accused see the book if he wants to see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking whether the book is an exhibit, because I see that this is a book that is called "Fire and Flood," published in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to have the book passed over to you. You can have a look at it and you can address us on it in due course if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm checking whether I have it available in the building. If I do, I'll make it available, I hope, by the break. If not, we'll try and get the book -- we'll find a source for the book and try and get a copy as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 77, and it's just the middle -- sorry, 78, and let's take the Court to the source of the evidence that is to be given. Just yes or no to this: Did you have a conversation with somebody which touched on the business of orders being given in 1998 to local commanders in Kosovo? Did you have a conversation with somebody about that topic? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With whom did you have that conversation, and when?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leadership of the state security and my political colleagues, the president of my party. This was an entire series of talks with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were these conversations you had contemporaneous with events or were they after the event, when you were preparing your book?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the same time, contemporaneous. And later on I could only compare certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was said to you about the giving of orders to local commanders?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information from several sources, completely identical, that practically the so-called State Commission for Kosovo, consisting of seven or eight persons, commands over the situation in Kosovo. This is a parapolitical body which practically goes beyond the legal authorities of Yugoslavia and this meant carrying out Mr. Milosevic's personal will regarding the non-selective use of force, for unpurposeful means in terms of using force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come, then, directly, I think, to the body you've described as the State Commission, paragraph 83, over the page in the summary. When was this body formed; who, in your understanding, were its members?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, it was formed at a very early stage, during the first third of 1998. And the members of this commission, that has nothing to do with my opinion really, it's a question of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to interrupt you to invite you not to give us your opinion, which is exclusively the province of the Judges; just to tell us what you learnt at the time, as a matter of fact. But I interrupted you. The commission was formed early, and it comprised whom?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sainovic, Minic, Andjelkovic, Matkovic, the civilian part. And then the military part, Generals Pavkovic and Velickovic. Probably there were some other members, but these are the members that I know for sure, persons who I know for sure were members of the commission for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you speak of Markovic, which Markovic are you speaking of? What's his first name?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Matkovic. Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And his first name?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, I misheard. Can you tell us now a little bit about something that's been referred to but occasional, something called Horseshoe. Again, not opinion; just facts, please. Was there a plan that went by the name of Horseshoe?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that sense. This was a colloquial nickname for a completely different plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just so that we can understand the colloquial nickname, can you help us at all with when the name was first used and applied -- when it was first used?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what the plan meant. Now, when the term was used first, I really can't say, especially as it was the colloquial term applied and not an official one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did it mean?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an exercise plan of the Yugoslav army while it was the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, and the plan provided for training and exercise in case of an aggression on Yugoslavia from south-east Europe, and if the Albanian population should take the side of the foreign aggressor, then it would come into force. The army of Yugoslavia would come into force if these two conditions were met. They would take seven defensive positions and they would be geared towards neutralising the Albanian strongholds, and this exercise -- this plan was actually stored in an archive and then it was reactivated and would be reactivated with all the rest for taking action in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The seven defensive positions, can you -- are you in a position to list them, and if so, would you rather have a map to point them out for us?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we discussed this, I had this jotted down in writing, but as I haven't got the right to have my notes with me, I'm afraid that if I speak off the bat, I might make some mistakes. But they were seven directions making this semi-circle, and I think that those exact directions, the seven of them, are contained in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can see the ones that have been set out in paragraph 85, at the top of page 15. I don't know if the Chamber would want to see those places, if I'm allowed to refer to them, on a map. We can either use the map that's at the front of the atlas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I find it useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I can just make mine, I think, available. This may do. It may be too big for the overhead. But if you can just look at this. I'm just going to read you some --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you point them out with the pointer, please, Mr. Tanic. First of all, there's the -- something called -- well, that's Mount Deravica. Can you just point that out for us?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but if the Court agrees, I'm not a military expert and I'd prefer not to indicate something on the map that I haven't already practiced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I'll abandon that exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see how he lists it and we can get somebody else to do it maybe later. Thank you very much, I'll take the map back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, do you know, one way or another, whether there was any intention or expression of intention at the time, the time of this conflict, to have anything to do with the Horseshoe plan?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, the basic purpose and intention of that plan was altered. There was no foreign aggression, and the Albanian population did not take the side of a foreign aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, back to where we were. Just yes or no: Was there any intention or expression at the time to have anything to do with this plan? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there general acceptance of its appropriate -- of its being an appropriate plan or not? Did anybody resist its use? Paragraph 87.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the peaks of power in the army and the security structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they accept it or did they reject it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't want to use the plan at all, because there was no external aggression or Albanian rebellion, or rather, that they should take the part and go to the side of the foreign aggressor, because it didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And from where did you learn that they were rejecting the use of such a plan, or from whom did you learn that they were rejecting the use of such a plan?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the army leadership. I would prefer not to mention any names. I don't want to harm those people, because many of them are under pressure anyway. So could we deal with it in a different way?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move to paragraph 88.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What's the objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is that the witness must answer the questions asked. What does it mean if he can say some nonsense like this and then he says that he can't tell you who he heard it from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a point you can make in due course. You can ask him again in cross-examination and we'll decide what to do about it. Meanwhile, the witness can go on in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 88, and this turns to the topic His Honour Judge Kwon was asking you about a little earlier. Were there some personnel changes at a very high level in the autumn of 1998? And just list them, please, for us.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. After the signing of the agreement between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Holbrooke on a peaceful settlement of the crisis in Kosovo, the military-political agreement, and the chiefs of the Security Services of Serbia and the Chief of the General Staff were replaced later on, Mr. Stanisic and the whole group of the leadership cadre. And Mr. Perisic as the head of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They were replaced by, and just give us the names of those who replaced them. Perisic was replaced by --? Paragraph 90.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And before we move from him, how had he ranked before this appointment? What were his political associations, if any?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. As to rank, I don't answer the question -- I don't understand the question. And as to his political connections, as far as I know, he was strongly connected to the JUL party. I can't tell you about rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Stanisic's replacement was whom?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radomir Markovic. We referred to him as Rade Markovic but his full name is Radomir Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What had been Radomir Markovic's previous political associations, if any?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very close personal ties with Mr. Milosevic and his family. Otherwise, before that, he didn't deal in any intelligence work but in the classical police force, or rather, the public Security Service, the public police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SJB, as we call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And then Dimitrijevic's replacement, can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I don't want to give you an incorrect answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 91. In 1998, did something happen in relation to what I think you described as economic materials in Kosovo? Just tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, economic materials was the term I used, and it relates to movable and immovable property, if I understood you correctly. Is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were material -- economic materials, yes, then that did take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what sort of materials are you talking of and what time are you talking of, so that we can see how far it was before NATO's intervention.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there might be a misunderstanding, but we'll be able to ascertain. If we're talking about allocations for Kosovo, then immovables are combat vehicles belonging to the artillery, light artillery, tanks, and that is the materiel, in fact, of the army that must not be used against civilians because in this case the Albanians were citizens of Yugoslavia. If that's what you mean, combat resources. Now, if you're referring to economic material of a different nature, we could perhaps clarify that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Gasoline reserves?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assumed that there was a misunderstanding. That's right. For several months before the conflict with the NATO pact, fuel, strategic fuel reserves, they were transported to lesser reservoirs all over Serbia, both belonging to military and economic organisations. So the strategic fuel reserves were transferred to other places several months before, between the conference in Rambouillet, or rather, the Milosevic/Holbrooke agreement and the conference in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Paragraph 94, conversations you've had, but I want you to move carefully and listen to the questions carefully, please. Vladimir Stambuk, remind us of his position at the time.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vice-president of the government of Serbia, one of the vice-presidents, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, did you - just yes or no - did you have a conversation with him in I think 1998 about the problems with Kosovar Albanians? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where and, so far as you can be precise, when?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation was between the British ambassador, Mr. Donnelly, the German ambassador, Mr. Gruber, Mr. Stambuk and myself, and this took place on the premises of the German embassy, and I think that that was two weeks before the Milosevic/Holbrooke agreement, perhaps ten days prior to that, a brief time before the Holbrooke/Milosevic agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. The topic of the conversation, in the most general terms first?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The topic of conversation was how to avoid NATO intervention against Yugoslavia, because at that time the danger already loomed over the country that the intervention might take place, and could Holbrooke prevent this intervention? Those were the general lines discussed. Or rather, whether a Milosevic/Holbrooke agreement would come into being at all to prevent the intervention, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In other words, I think a particular observation made by Stambuk that you can tell us about in the course of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stambuk did make an observation which I heard from others as well. I quoted Mr. Stambuk by way of one example. He made the observation to the two foreign ambassadors, ambassadors of NATO-pact countries, that official Belgrade had nothing against a small-scale bombing operation by NATO, and of course I reacted to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he go on to qualify and explain what would happen at all, if there was a small bombing operation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't carry on his explanations in the face of these two ambassadors, the ambassadors of Great Britain and Germany, because I asked him to go to one side and to stop that kind of conversation, and then he explained it to me. The explanation he gave was -- actually, I asked him how was it possible for any official - and as we knew each other, I was free to ask him that - any official to say that official Belgrade had nothing against a limited bombing? That kind of observation was completely taboo because that means an invitation to them to bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to expand on the answers, because we just want an account of what was said. So you made those observations to him, and what, if any, further explanation did he give to you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he answered me by saying that I didn't understand certain things, but the president of my party, Mr. Mihajlovic -- that is, he said that a small-scale bombing would be a great pretext and alibi for us to continue with the persecution of Albanians and the Serb opposition as well, because in times of war, nobody can ask anything. So he advised me to convey to the president of my party that we go back to the ruling coalition and to stop resisting attempts of this artificial construction of a war conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've used in your evidence the phrase "continue with the persecution of Albanians." Obviously it's a long time ago, and don't guess if you can't, but can you help at all with exactly what he said about the Albanians and/or persecution of them?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said to finish ethnic cleansing, to have a pretext for completing the ethnic cleansing of the Albanians or to throw them out of the territory of Yugoslavia, and I heard words to that effect from others as well, mentioned in other documents, irrespective of my views and opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say in relation to that last topic but also the earlier topic about the acceptability of --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To that effect about other nations as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself in the previous sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question, then. You say in relation to the last Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. topic but also in relation to the earlier topic of the acceptability of small-scale bombing, that others said similar things to what Mr. Stambuk had said. Can you give us the names of any of the others who said such things, either at this meeting in the embassy or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a very large group of people, from Mr. Milovan Bojic to Mr. -- that is to say, various people from the SPS, leaders, Mr. Milutinovic himself. I just can't enumerate all these people, there were a lot of them. And they were all closed talks. They all spoke about this little bit of bombing as if this wouldn't make a problem. Of course, not in their public statements, but in their private conversations. Not only then but on many other occasions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 96. There's a man called Bogdan Tomas. Who was he in 1998? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I ask us to leave this question for a private session, to protect these people? Not because I don't wish to answer, but I don't wish to place anybody in a precarious position. These people are in a sufficiently precarious position already when they want to say what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I put that on one side, then, and come back at the end to a collective, if there is to be any private session, a collective private session? And that, I think, will take care of 97 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You may have touched on this yesterday, but just tidy it up, if you wouldn't mind, today: Did you get to learn of the accused's attitude towards information gathering on the KLA generally and about his attitude towards the surrender to this institution of any who had committed crimes against the Serbs? Just yes or no to that. Did you get to learn of his attitude?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From where did you learn of his attitude? From him himself or from others?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Give us the range of people and their jobs, if you can, from whom you learned of his attitude.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leadership of the security structures, the military leadership, the socio-political structures, and I can name them at a private session. That will be no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the accused's attitude towards learning about the KLA and handing them over to this institution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this is important evidence. I think better that you come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider the whole question of a closed session in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In that case, I think, although part of 1998 may be separable, if I just come back to that generally. We can then go over to page 18, and I think probably it will be better if I deal with this major element on page 18 later. I'll come back to that, but not in closed session, Your Honour, but I think in open session, but I'll come back to it. Paragraph 101.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, did you learn of the conduct of certain operations against the KLA in 1998, and in particular, of one involving the Jashari family? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any pattern -- according to your information, was there any pattern in the way some of these operations were mounted, in particular, in terms of the size of the initial action taken against the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a terrible pattern in opposition to everybody -- anything that could be read in the leadership of the army, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The pattern that you identified or that's been identified was what?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This pattern consisted of the fact that they should allow a smaller number of Serb victims first in order to raise tensions, and then to launch a massive non-selective use of force against the Albanian population much greater than would be necessary for eliminating the rebels and to destroy civilian lives and civilian buildings. This pattern, not only with the Jashari family was used, but in Decani as well, with certain variations. But usually it was the overly great use of force and unselective use of force, which was contrary to the rules and regulations of the police force as well, the rules of service of the police force and the laws generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you've given the pattern. We'll come back to the two particular locations you've identified briefly in a few minutes. But as against this, and from your understanding of the Security Service with which you had contact, what was the appropriate way to deal with terrorists who would be in a civilian community? Paragraph 105.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not my understanding. There is procedure that is prescribed, and that procedure, combat procedure, that's what I'm talking about, not legal procedure. Combat procedure was dovetailed with the law and ascribed in the rules of services with respect to the deployment of the services, at all attempts to divide civilians from terrorists, particularly under circumstances where we know that many terrorists do have, as a rule, resort to using civilians as a human shield or things of that kind. There are technical means and logistics to combat that and the equipment of our units. After that, what is done is to arrest them at all costs rather than killing them, and you can carry out arrests in various ways. You have combat means for effecting an arrest and taking people into custody, but at any right, the mass use of force against civilians would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that's enough. And just this last question from paragraph 106. Were units at that time available equipped with the necessary materials and equipment to deal with terrorists in this proper and formal way?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nor were they equipped with the materiel, nor did they have the necessary cadres, and so those were one of the criticisms that Stanisic and Perisic made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be my misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were criticised for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the units at that time have, for example, tear gas or material like that that might have been usable against terrorists in a controlled way, of the way you've explained a few paragraphs before?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, in their warehouses, but they didn't use them, and that's why the misunderstanding came about. They didn't use them on the terrain, in the field. They did have all the equipment necessary and logistics, theoretically speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've given two examples, Jashari family and Decani. As to any detail of what happened at either of those events or incidents, what was your source of information, in general?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, once again, the leadership of the State Security Service and the army, and this can be brought up at a private session. And some people who were there on the spot as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But passing beyond your sources, then, to what they told you, who did you understand to be in charge of these missions at those times?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we first discussed the problems at length. They didn't tell me that once, we had an ongoing discussion about that kind of problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're not listening -- you are listening. It's my mistake for not getting the question properly. Who in the leadership was in charge of these missions that bore this characteristic you've described? Paragraph 102.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to all practical terms, it was the civilian part of the staff, and this is mentioned in General Perisic's letter as well. To all practical purposes, it was that part that conveyed orders from Mr. Milosevic and his closest associates, not from institutions, but from them as local commanders, according to my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can you give us the names of the civilian individuals who were responsible for these particular missions?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly it was Mr. Nikola Sainovic's name that was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Mr. Vlajko Stojilkovic as well, but the gentleman has died since, so I don't like to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if that would prove to be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'd be grateful for your assistance. Perhaps you can reflect on it during the adjournment, and also the amicus, is the course which we should follow with this evidence. Some of it's important but based on sources which either are not given or are said to be given in private session. The question is the value of that evidence and whether it should be admitted at all. But perhaps you would reflect on it. We'll adjourn now. We're going to adjourn, Mr. Milosevic. We'll hear you afterwards. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, I should have explained this to you, since you may not have followed the procedural argument, that the question of naming any names is a matter on which you will be guided by counsel, and in due course it may be the Trial Chamber will have to make a ruling on the subject, but you'll be told what to do and what your position is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply did not understand that, and that is why I asked for instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court wants to discuss the utility of a private session now or whether we should get through the rest of the evidence and deal with it all at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's get on with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have a copy of the book. It's actually a private copy of Mr. Shin, but he's prepared to make it available if not to donate it to the greater good. It's the only copy we have got at the moment, so can I make it available so the accused can look at it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've flagged it, or rather, Ms. Graham has flagged it at the two letters that are going to be produced. We can consider its status as an exhibit or whatever later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 107. No. That falls for the same consideration later, I'm afraid. Let's move on to paragraph 108, to events during the NATO bombing. Did you, in the course of the NATO bombing, have any face-to-face meetings with the accused?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was communication with the accused, through official channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But did you have any face-to-face meeting with him, at receptions and things of that sort, in April of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a meeting that could prove anything. The accused is denying everything. I cannot prove this. I can prove all the rest. So let that be my answer to this question. Indirect communication through official channels, communications between the governments of Serbia and Yugoslavia respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, I'm just going to press you. The question of how things are proved is a matter for the Court really. Just yes or no: Did you have conversations with the accused in April 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the spring of 1999, yes, on a very brief occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: It is quite hard to prove that now, and I would kindly ask that, if possible, this also remains for this other part, when these specific matters will be dealt with, names and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Paragraph 110. In the course of the NATO bombing, the -- did you learn - just yes or no - about some of the things that were happening in the course of the bombing; for example, deployments of the armed forces, aircraft -- anti-aircraft positions, that sort of thing? Did you learn about any of those sorts of things?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, absolutely. Personal insight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What appeared to be the main strategy about, so far as an approach to NATO was concerned, from what you understood?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what I understood and found out, the main strategy was to procrastinate as much as possible and to extend the war with NATO for as long as possible, to the detriment of own country, and then the civilian loss of lives and the civilian destruction would constitute a kind of moral victory over NATO, and that strategy was clearly enunciated. That can be proven as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I think 113 will fall in the same category probably as some of the earlier passages. But over the page: Did you have contact with the Russian foreign minister at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I beg your pardon. This must be a mistake. In everything I said, there was not a single indication that I could have had that kind of contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. My mistake. Yes. We'll have to move on from that, I think. As to civilian buildings, what happened to civilian buildings - paragraph 115 - in the course of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were used for military purposes, and this was unauthorised. I'll give an example. I'm talking about the command of the town of Belgrade, the city of Belgrade, which was at two different locations. I personally saw this. I can mention both locations. There is no problem with that. The elementary school of Sveti Sava in the street of Marsala Tulbuhina and also the department store company in Marsala Tulbuhina Street as well. They are very close to one another. The one is a civilian company, the other an elementary school. And the command of the city of Belgrade was relocated to these locations and the officers who were in command of the city of Belgrade for long periods, during the day wore civilian clothes. And then tanks for a while, they were deployment around the church of Sveti Sava, Saint Sava, and then when people started complaining about this, then they were moved from there. But as for the command, the headquarters of the defence of the city of Belgrade, I personally saw where they were relocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 117. RTS, Radio Television Serbia, did you get some information about that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have information about the bombing of the RTS building with two days before and two days later, and I communicated this through official channels to the command or defence, or rather, to Mr. Milosevic, who at that time was the supreme commander of the defence, so he had to be informed, and I have doubt that he must have been informed. The building was not evacuated and civilians were left there on purpose so that they would lose their lives, and I know that there were several sources of information with regard to this RTS building bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The SDB, did it have information about future targets other than whatever you may have acquired from somewhere else? Did it have other sources of information?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were other sources of information, two or three different types of sources of information, quite valid, without any kind of espionage involved. I'm not referring to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was this continuously provided to the accused or was there any change in the pattern of provision to him, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He absolutely had to obtain this information, and his behaviour showed that he did have this information and that sometimes he would evacuate the population and sometimes he would not. It depended on what was useful for him. Also this refers to goods, property, not only the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the SDB continue to provide him information throughout the war or not?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your role at this time was to do what, and on whose authority?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the decision or opinion. Please take into account one of these two wordings. The opinion or the decision of the united defence of the town of Belgrade and the SDB. I went abroad twice during the war. I cannot call this being sent out on official business, but the explanation was that I should do my best, depending on the people I know, to investigate, to investigate - I emphasise that word - the possibility of bringing the conflict with NATO to an end as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to an end. Mr. Nice, I'm concerned about this evidence, based on what are described as sources. And the question really is: Of what value is it to the Trial Chamber to have evidence of that sort?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. That, of course, falls for determination when we -- in part when we look at the next thing. As to this particular passage of evidence, he's told us what he was doing. I now need to know on what authority he was doing it and then we come to another concrete piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this stage, I think we're in a slightly different territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, but if you would stick to the concrete for the moment and in due course we can consider the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you've told us what you were doing. You were abroad on official business, investigating the possibility of bringing the conflict to an end. Whose authority was it that you should do that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The united staff of the defence of the town of Belgrade and the State Security Service. There was no way of leaving Belgrade during the war for private purposes only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were able to leave Belgrade to do the functions that you've described; yes?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
