utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But being officially seen off and met by the Security Service at the border with Hungary, and that is where I left the country, and there are official records of that. So this was an official procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. As a result of those missions, or that mission, did you have any proposals that you were able to advance?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One or more than one?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One. One. It was one proposal that was figuring prominently throughout this time. Various variations of it, but basically one proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when did that proposal come about, first?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, mid-April 1999, at the latest, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a letter that we may be able to produce from Mr. Lilic to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that letter have a bearing on this potential agreement, or is it a reflection of it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand this question as being addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it is addressed to you. There's a letter --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a letter from Mr. Lilic in May of 1999, and does that bear out what you're saying about the offer of an agreement that you came back with?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it does bear it out. The spirit and many concrete provisions of that proposal as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, that letter is in the annex or the appendices to the book that we've just provided to the accused. Had you ever seen the letter before seeing it in that book?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I did not see the letter in the book either. I found out about it from an interview that Mr. Lilic gave to the weekly called Vrema, about three months ago, and I saw that it coincided to a great degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm proposing to deal with that letter at a later stage in the evidence, by another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But can you tell us, just in the shortest possible form, please: What was the agreement that you -- what were the elements of the agreement that you were party to proposing?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I was not putting it together. I did not have the mandate to put anything together. The elements of this agreement were the following: The unilateral ceasefire of all combat activities of the army of Yugoslavia and the special units of the MUP for a 24-hour period, except for cases of self-defence. After that, the suspension of combat activities of NATO for a period of 24 hours. And then a longer unilateral ceasefire by the army of Yugoslavia and the combat units of MUP, except for cases of self-defence. And a longer suspension of bombing by NATO. In the meantime, the urgent initiation of political dialogue with Kosovar Albanians, specifically with Mr. Rugova, about resolving political problems related to Kosovo. The Pristina Corps remains in Kosovo, and peace troops enter Kosovo and they possibly -- no, not possibly. They do cooperate with the Pristina Corps. And then after a lasting ceasefire and after a peace agreement is reached, then the economic community would help the reconstruction of Kosovo and then peace troops would enter under the UN flag, and official Belgrade would be free to influence the composition of the peace troops of the UN in the following sense: That there would not be too many people from NATO countries there, so that this would be a bit of a face-saving formula for Yugoslavia. That is, in rough terms, the content of the peace proposal, and there was not only one of them, and they were shown to President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a proposal for a ceasefire on Catholic Easter, and was there a linkage of that, or temporal linkage of that, with the release of some American soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was. That was also one of the variants of this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that discussed by you and your party leader Mihajlovic, and did that lead you to making a telephone call? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To whom was the telephone call made?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First we addressed a proposal in writing to Mr. Milutinovic, and then, after that, the president of my party spoke on the telephone to Mr. Milutinovic in connection with a reply to that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you in a position to hear one side or both sides of that telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. Both. It's no secret; the speakerphone was on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was said by Mihajlovic to Milutinovic and what was said by Milutinovic in reply?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. Milosevic clearly made it known that he would accept a ceasefire for Catholic Easter, and it is not only that we knew about it, but also Mr. Sedano [phoen], the Secretary of State of the Vatican.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... background. You really must focus on the questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The phone call now, please: What was said?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, our question was: Why was there no ceasefire for Catholic Easter when it was promised? Because Catholic Easter was already in the past. And also, the freeing of the three American soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reply?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the answer that Mr. Milutinovic gave was that he said there would be a ceasefire but a little later on, because he said we - and he meant Belgrade - we have not finished the job done there yet, meaning Kosovo, and that it would take place for the Orthodox Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is how much later?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't specific, Mr. Milutinovic. He said, "We haven't finished the job down there in Kosovo yet, and once we do finish it, then we'll see to it."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think at one stage you had a conversation with the president of the Assembly, Tomic, about the peace negotiations of which you were aware. Just yes or no: Did Mr. Tomic seem aware of those negotiations at all? Had they been communicated to him?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but with others too; Vuk Draskovic, in the first place, who was the vice-premier. Perhaps there was a mistake in my basic -- that is to say, technical mistake, because there was far more communication with Mr. Draskovic as the vice-premier of the Yugoslav government at the time, but also with Tomic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 131. No. Paragraph 131 will have to come later, if at all. Paragraph 137, just a few odd details now, please, Mr. Tanic. The Republic of Serbian police, did they have any particular characteristics? Did they have any particular source from which they were drawn which would identify them in a particular way?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question and be more specific? I'm not quite sure I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The Republic of Serbian police, how integrated were they with the other agencies of law enforcement? How separate were they?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The composition of the public Security Service was integrated. However, the composition of the specialised units were not integrated into those basic forms. But I still don't think I've understood your question fully, at least not precisely enough to give you a full answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to pursue the matter. I'll move on to something else. The control of the MUP -- no, I think you've actually dealt with that already. That's paragraph 138. Paragraph 148. Special units, again, then, picking up on that. Did you see anything of those special units yourself at the time with which we're concerned?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. The special units and the police, they were referred to as the JSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you learn - just yes or no - by whom they were controlled?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In particular, by whom they were controlled when they were operating in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, using his private chain of command through Sainovic and Rade Markovic and Vlajko Stojilkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 149. Did you have any conversation, I think, with Perisic about these units? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific once again when you say "special units," because there are special units both in the army and the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be difficult for me to discuss special police units with Perisic, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is my error, I think. Can I come back to it? Did you have a conversation - yes or no - with Perisic about military equipment going to the police? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you have that? Was that contemporaneously or was that more recently, when you were sourcing material for your book?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the time when I was preparing the material for my book and comparing my knowledge from the previous times with that of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just yes or no to this: Did Perisic tell you something of Milosevic's attitude towards this topic? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last line of paragraph 149: What did he tell you of Milosevic's attitude?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, similarly to what he had written in his letter. Let me be precise: That Mr. Milosevic kept asking him that the military equipment be issued to MUP units and that that military equipment would be used in combat operations, and Mr. Perisic, for many reasons, which he set out in the letter and one which he explained to me, was the deployment of this against the civilian population. There is no rule and regulation for this to be deployed and used against the inhabitants. And I'm referring here to heavy military materiel, equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any reference or consideration given to how the personnel would be dressed?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was mention of tanks, combat vehicles, infantry ones, and grenade launchers, 120 millimetres and over. And as I was told, Mr. Perisic said that that was absolutely impossible, and Mr. Milosevic responded to that and said that this would not be used by the army but by the police, so there was no danger of having the army blamed for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were local commanders, in your experience and understanding, able to arrest special unit members for wrongful acts?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Members of the reserve force as well. They also did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of the war, in general, what did you observe about the output of the local media, newspapers and so on?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I noticed a whole series of incorrect information put out, information which fanned the flames of war and masked the true results of the combat operations of the war; and this was true throughout 1998 and 1999. I'm talking about the official media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What sort of distortions were there?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the number of terrorists, for example, they were exaggerated, and the peaceful solutions were diminished. Our own victims were made less of, and generally, the whole operation was masked. So that kind of distortion, more or less, a distortion of the actual situation, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last paragraph. Some graves, mass graves, were found in Serbia. Did you have a conversation with someone about them?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, in the summer of 1999, when I was preparing my book and when we researched into the Serb and Albanian victims - where they were, where they could be found - and the second time was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I asked you who it was.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I'm a little confused now. Do you want me to answer now or can I ask to answer this in a private session, if we're going to have one? If not, then I can give an answer. There's no problem there. I don't wish to refrain from answering, I just want to see whether we're going to have this in open session or in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Obviously, I would prefer, if this is a name you can give publicly, that you give it publicly. Is there any reason not to give this name publicly?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. Very well. I won't be jeopardising these people, because there was an official investigation. Zoran Mijatovic, deputy head of the Security Services of Serbia, Dusan Mihajlovic, the Interior Minister of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did Mijatovic say about these mass graves that were found?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That there was an official investigation conducted by the MUP which indicates exactly the perpetrators, the locations, the sites themselves, but that for some reason that investigation was stopped. Otherwise I myself, when I was kidnapped, was exposed to torture --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm coming to that in a minute.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- linked to the mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I want to know a little bit more about what you learnt about the mass graves. There were mass graves. Mijatovic told you about it. Was there any connection made between those graves and any other finding or occurrence at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Mr. Mijatovic, but Mr. Mihajlovic as well, the Internal Affairs Minister. They merely told me the results of the investigation, as far as it had got. Now, could you clarify what you mean by the connection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had a vehicle been found in the Danube River? Is there a connection between one and the other?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a vehicle had been found in the Danube, at a place called Vitusi Puteljak, near Tekija, and it was a vehicle which Mr. Keta took from the customs department and gave to the units of public security to transport the bodies, just prior to the NATO intervention in Kosovo and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did Mijatovic tell you about all this? And then we'll turn on to the circumstances of your leaving Yugoslavia. What did Mijatovic tell you about all this?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, that -- actually, he didn't tell me his opinion, but the results of the investigation, that there was a clear connection between Mr. Milosevic and the order to mask -- cover up the graves, and that these bodies had been brought in before the NATO intervention and that the origin of those bodies, unfortunately, was that in the units of Sreten Lukic and not the state security of Serbia, and that that is why a cover-up was under force, a cover-up for the truth and the mass graves, although our official organs were well aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were these the only mass graves of which you learned or were there others?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just discussed one. I didn't have the psychological strength to go into the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sreten Lukic at the time the head of the MUP in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come back now, then, to deal with the circumstances in which you came to leave Yugoslavia. What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after I had started preparing my book and sourcing the material for the book linked to Kosovo and the crimes connected with Kosovo, a short time after that, and after my telephone conversations had been intercepted and that they came to learn that I was preparing a book which would be expounding the kind of things I am saying here today, I was quite simply kidnapped in the street, and two hours later so was my wife, at the beginning of October 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long were you held for, altogether?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were both kidnapped, drugged, and taken to two different private prisons, where we spent two days each, my wife and myself, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to you in prison? I don't want to distress you and we don't need to go into it in great detail, not because it may not have been --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and to save time too. But it was torture of the Latin American variety, from administering injections to being beaten up, to be suffocated, and I'm building up this source and these materials for my book, but I don't want to present them all. But there was an attempt to show a sort of non-existent international plot and conspiracy against Mr. Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the -- were you questioned?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can call it questioning, if beating with a sack over your head and being drugged can be called questioned, then I was questioned. That's how I was questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was the topic of the questioning? What was its apparent direction?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is page 18 of the summary. I'm sorry not to have directed you to it earlier.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was geared towards knowing why I was investigating this, the Serb graves and the mass graves, why I was in contact with the SDB, do I really want to write this book, and so on and so forth. And around public -- private matters of that kind. Secondly, we discussed the investigations. That was the reason for my being tortured, because they wanted me to acknowledge the so-called conspiracy against Mr. Milosevic, his private security, and so on, British conspiracy, and that I had contacts with intelligence services. And then they tortured me and my wife and wanted us to say that it was -- we were engaged in espionage. Now, we managed to survive this torture. I was drugged, my wife was not drugged. She was only beaten. And then the next stage of the investigation took a somewhat different turn. In that next stage, these individuals said that they were the people who wanted to overthrow Milosevic, in fact, and that everything I went through was in fact a test on their part to see how fit I was to survive and that they wanted me to link them up to the people from the British intelligence service so that we could cooperate to toppling Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were released. How much longer after your release did you stay in Serbia at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was released two hours prior to the abortive attempt to assassinate Vuk Draskovic, and I stayed on for another month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then eventually you were able to leave the country?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, legally, because I saw that a killing was being prepared this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm going to pause there, and perhaps we can deal with the other topic in general. Might it be convenient to deal with that itself in private session? Because names may get mentioned. The argument about the admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the matter should be dealt with, if possible, in public, because it's a matter of principle, without mentioning any names. If you want to refer to the statement, perhaps that would be a convenient way to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My notes would suggest that this issue relates or would become relevant to page 2, paragraph 3. Now, I'm not sure about that one. That's the one I'm not sure about. I've got an annotation at the foot of paragraph 3 which may relate to this sort of material. And then the rest of the material turned up today, and I have annotations starting at page 17, paragraph 96. 97, 98. Then at page 20, paragraph 108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about paragraph 87, page 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't note that one at the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could check it out later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. Now, it seems to me that when we come to page 17 -- I've dealt with 17. When we come to page 20, the issue arises in a similar way in respect to paragraph 113, but rather differently in relation to paragraph 108. I'm passed a note that Your Honour is quite right about the earlier page, paragraph 87. Paragraph 113 is the usual problem. Paragraph 108 I think is a different problem, because paragraph 108 is not dependent upon anxiety about the well-being of others, and it's a matter perhaps for the witness to give further explanation of his reasons for not wishing to give this evidence publicly. It may be convenient if I asked him about that once more, so that we can understand the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that he can understand the difference as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, as you realise, the Chamber is about to consider evidence that turns on what you were told by other people, you being concerned to protect their names in order to protect them from risk. Now, before we come to deliberate -- or before the Chamber comes to deliberate on that and to hear argument about it, there's another passage of evidence which related to the conversation or encounter certainly you had with the accused in April 1999. What's your reason, so that we can have it, for preferring to give that evidence in private session, given that you've said everything else you've had to say about the accused publicly and given also that, as we know, you're protected in these proceedings by facial distortion in order that your future security may be properly preserved? So what's your concern about the evidence in April 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my overall relationship to the Tribunal. I wish to show maximum respect. Mr. Milosevic rejects everything I say, beginning with my very existence in these affairs onwards. So I'm ready to give the Tribunal just those statements which I can confirm by at least two or three independent sources, so that it becomes quite clear that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, I'm going to stop you there. It's the Tribunal and the lawyers who address it who decide issues of law, sufficiency of evidence, and matters of that sort, not for you. So the question is quite simple. There's no reason not to give that evidence; if you don't wish to give it, just say you don't wish to give it, and then we'll move on, but there's no reason in what you've advanced for not giving the evidence. Are you prepared to give that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not because there is official communication with Milosevic at that time. That is sufficient for public -- for a public statement, public testimony. Nothing changes in this communication. He did the same thing he did in the private communication, which I can't prove. So it's the same thing. I have not cut short this information to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Are you prepared, then - it's for the Tribunal to weigh - are you prepared to tell us what was said at that meeting in April 1999, please?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am prepared to state what was said in official communication with Mr. Milosevic, and that is the same substance as the other kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is pointless going on fencing like this. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Well, I think that comes to an end of that paragraph. Paragraph 113 falls into the same category, the general category, and page 131 [sic] certainly, and I think that's all I have. The Tribunal is in a position to provide closed session under -- or in camera proceedings under Rule 75, subject also to Rule 79, and Rule 79 is fairly narrow. It deals with closed session for public order or morality. Safety, security or non-disclosure of the identity of a victim or witness is provided in Rule 75, or the protection of the interests of justice, which is rather more broad. It may be that it's the protection of the interests of justice that is one thing that the Chamber should have in mind in considering the present position. When we come back to 75, making sure it hasn't been amended, because I still haven't got an up-to-date version with me. I'll read from the amended version: "A Chamber may hold an in camera proceeding to determine whether to order..." and then "(i) measures to prevent disclosure to the public or the media of the identity or the whereabouts of a victim or witness or of persons related to or associated with a victim or witness by means such as..." and then it runs through protective measures not including closed session. And then without listing a series of criteria, identifies (ii), "closed session in accordance with Rule 79." And then (iii), "appropriate measures to facilitate the testimony of vulnerable victims and witnesses, such as one-way closed-circuit television." So that looked at in the most technical sense, simply because Rule 79 is not given further criteria in Rule 75, the category of persons identified in 75(B)(i), which is inclusive of persons related to or associated with a victim or witness might not, prima facie, cover this particular circumstance, although if it would be appropriate, and we would invite you to say it really must be, to incorporate that wider reasoning for closed sessions, then it could be. And in any event, the interests of justice -- it's not described as the interests of justice, it's described as the protection of the interests of justice -- would allow what this witness seeks. He seeks to be able to give his evidence in certain particulars, withholding from the full public scrutiny the names of people from whom he derived information. The names will, of course, be known to the accused and may be provided by the accused to those assisting him in the preparation of his defence as to the amici, and in those circumstances, there is no unfairness on the accused. His rights are fully preserved. He's able to cross-examine. It might be necessary to have discrete areas of closed session or private session testimony for the cross-examination, but he's quite able to deal with the case, and there is no loss to him. The witness's concerns, of course, reflect that there are others who may hold views contrary to his, who may be concerned by illegal means to thwart these proceedings, and who would thus pose a very real threat to sources of information upon which he acted. The Court knows of the concerns we've had about the dissemination of information, but so far, apart from the matters I've drawn to your attention in the past, nothing further has come to light. And now, of course, the accused's assistants are committed to the Rules of the Tribunal. So there's a realistic prospect of material heard in private session not leaking out, and the accused has told you himself on an earlier occasion that his word is enough for these things and he doesn't have to be bound by your Rules. So that the witness identifies a real distinction between what is provided here in -- or could be provided here in private session, to make the trial fair, and what could only be provided, in his judgement, publicly, at risk to those individuals. My understanding is that there have been earlier occasions of selective private-session evidence being held, I think once in the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a difficulty. We can order part of the evidence to be given in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was saying also for the protection of people other than witnesses, although I think in the Tadic case it was probably for a relation. And with this sort of case and with these sorts of issues, although we are doing everything we can to ensure that everything is given in public in this case, this sort of evidence, which is potentially valuable or very valuable to the Tribunal, does expose certain individuals to risk. Now, there's, of course, a difference between -- and it's a difference that the accused has himself really articulated - between naming the people, whether they are named as co-perpetrators or whether they are simply people closely associated with government at the time, and he's named those entirely straightforwardly. There's a difference between those people and the functionaries who don't fall within those categories, who may not themselves be associated with any wrongdoings of the kind charged here but whose provision of information to this witness, in the public good, could be deeply damaging to them. And so we would invite you to say that it's entirely proper, for these comparatively limited number of instances, to allow private-session testimony, in both direct and cross-examination, for the Chamber in due course to decide what weight to place on that evidence if it decides that there is any diminution in its value by reason of its being in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, wouldn't you say that the Rules are primarily designed for the protection of victims and witnesses and that insofar as the protection of other persons is concerned, there would be a higher threshold to be met to gain that protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I'd agree with the second proposition, although I think the first proposition is clearly right, because the Rules, when they were being drafted, probably had victims and witnesses more specifically in focus. But I would respectfully doubt whether a court would operate on a higher threshold of safety or danger -- a higher threshold of danger or lower threshold of safety, if it was aware that testimony was about to be given which would expose someone to real risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you know, one reason for the higher threshold might be the availability of reliable evidence to the Chamber. That evidence would certainly be easier to get in relation to a victim and witness than in relation to other persons. So it's a question of how will the Chamber be satisfied as to the need for protection of a person who is neither a victim nor witness? So it's a question of evidence to satisfy the Chamber, and it seems to me that it would be much easier to get that evidence in relation to victims and witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that's a different proposition, and I think the threshold of evidential material may typically be different. Yes. I don't necessarily disagree with that. But it's the very nature of the material that the witness is providing here that would - and we can see it from the summary - which would point to the obvious danger that providers of that material might be in, given the nature of people who still hold very strong views in a country that has, as we know, quite a high level of crimes recently associated -- killings, indeed, recently associated, or comparatively recently, associated with these events. People have disappeared, and, as we know, people have been shot, and so on, for one reason or another, but it's of that sort of country. So if we look at just one or two of the particular passages, and I think probably page 17 is as good as any, without going into the detail of either the sources or the topics upon which they were providing information to this witness. Paragraph 96, but perhaps more particularly, 97, one can see particular places referred to. And then I think also if you go over to page 107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Paragraph 107, page 19. And then finally, page 22, paragraph 131. One can readily imagine how people providing information on those topics might very well be at considerable risk from the intervention of others but how their provision in private session will mean that the accused is well able to conduct and have a fair trial. I think that's all I can say on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is an issue where we should look at the Rules first of all. I note His Honour Judge Robinson's observations about Rule 75, which does seem, on our reading, to be a provision more directly connected with protection of victims and witnesses. When one looks at 75(B)(i), again victim or witness or of persons related to or associated with a victim or witness, looks rather to deal with more of a witness's personal situation as he finds himself in a courtroom at that time, the protection of others who are close to him. And we would say that this provision is more specifically designed for the witness who comes from a place where his family is, his associates, people related to him, could in some way be affected by his giving particular evidence. That isn't the case here with this particular witness and his circumstances. It is not the normal one and would fall outside Rule 75 in its general application. We say it's more Rule 79 issue that the Prosecution are bringing here, relying more upon the protection of the interests of justice. This is an issue where an accused is entitled to have evidence which a witness gives in public and to be accountable for that which he says. Reliance upon sources which are not identified publicly does put him at a disadvantage, although the names may be given in closed session and identities able to be investigated by his associates in preparation of his defence. This kind of material can also help an accused if it is made public, because others associated with these events and information at the time are able to scrutinise what is said and able to offer themselves to a defendant as witnesses on his behalf if they disagree with what is said. The equality of arms principle does, to a great extent, require, as much as possible, for a Defence to be in public so it is capable of being analysed by external sources, scrutinised, and witnesses to be held accountable for what they have said publicly. The difficulty is, with a closed session, that that becomes less likely and it can affect the equality of arms which the Court must seek to achieve in providing a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, Mr. Tanic. You want to say something. This is really a legal argument, as you must understand, but if there's something you want to say about your evidence, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I'm not going to interfere in the legal argument. This has to do with my evidence. I believe that this question is unduly hampering my testimony, and therefore I am prepared to state in public what I said I would like to say in public [sic] session. I don't want to make the work of the Trial Chamber, of the Office of the Prosecutor, more difficult, so I'm prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's very helpful. I'll go back over those paragraphs. I do, for my own reasons, and in order to communicate something to the accused, need about 30 seconds in private session. It's got nothing to do with the current testimony, it has something to do with the witness. May I do that literally now, while we've broken the testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Well, I think I'm going to go as swiftly as I can. We're going to revisit certain topics that you've given us some answers on earlier. Again, briefly, please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 87, page 15. You spoke of the Horseshoe plan, and indeed you spoke of the peaks of power - those were your terms - who opposed it. Who were the peaks of power who opposed and refused to implement this plan?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army -- the use of the army and police for these purposes were opposed by Jovica Stanisic, head of state security of Serbia, Zoran Mijatovic in the capacity of his deputy, that is to say, head of the centre of the services of state security of Belgrade. That is practically 80 per cent of the SDB. General Momcilo Perisic, in his capacity as chief of general staff. General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic, in his capacity as head of the intelligence service of the army. It is known as the KOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then there are other persons as well. I'm sorry, there are other persons who also opposed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Go on.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the leading persons in the operations of the SDB and the military security. Then -- I have to pull myself together in order to recollect all of this. Then politicians from the so-called Reformist Group within the government of Serbia, or rather, within the Serbian and Yugoslavia political scene. Mr. Zoran Lilic, Mr. Dusan Mihajlovic, Mr. Nebojsa Covic, people who were popularly known as the Reformists. That would be a group of people. Perhaps I've forgotten someone. It's a broader group but I really don't want to burden you with more of this. They always opposed this in a substantiated manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'd like to find out, if the witness is able to tell us, what was the basis for their opposition to the Horseshoe Plan, very briefly. And just let me tell you: My recollection is that your evidence is that the essence of the plan was that if an aggressor attacked from a particular point, and if the Kosovar Albanian population supported the aggressor, then particular action would be taken. So the plan was really based on a hypothesis. So in the context of that hypothesis, can you help me as to what was the basis for the opposition to the plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall gladly answer, but I have to make a point. Horseshoe plan did not exist as an official name. I said that quite precisely. So there was an abuse of this old military plan for exercises and training. It was not a new Horseshoe plan. This was just a colloquial nickname, as I had put it. And now I'm going to answer your question. The point of their opposition was that, first and foremost, there was no external aggression and therefore there was no Albanian population that sided with the foreign aggressor. Therefore, there was less need to use the army in such a large scale and all these special units. Additional reason for their opposition was that the problem of Kosovo could have had been resolved through political means and through selective force, and that was something that was known two or three years prior to that, including me. I knew that. And this entire group, and I had opposed this, of course, at a lower level than the group of people I just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 17, paragraph 96. You had started to tell us about knowledge of the detail of the KLA forces. How well was their strength known, and who talked to you about this in Belgrade in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of what I know, when speaking about the top echelons of the State Security Service, is based on working conversations. These are not private conversations or dinner-table conversation. This is with -- these are conversations with Mr. Zoran Mijatovic, the deputy of Mr. Jovica Stanisic, and also head of the State Security Services for Belgrade, and also with his other associates. I think that identifying this one name is sufficient. And this name became known to the general public later. It was mentioned that, according to the assessments of the MUP and the SDB, there were 2.000 terrorists at that time. Excuse me, Mr. Nice; which period are we actually discussing? 1998 or before that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you went to Belgrade on leave in 1998, did you have conversations with someone about the strength of the KLA, particularly in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 1998. I have to correct myself. The KLA was more than 2.000-strong. I was referring to the period 1997, 1996. I'm sorry. This was inadvertent. So as for 1998, I discussed that with the officers, or rather, the officials of the SDB. I mentioned one name. And also a man who was in charge of SDB operations down there in the region of Djakovica. His name is Bogdan Tomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was he able to tell you about the strength of the KLA and about the Security Services' level of knowledge of where they lived and so on?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to insist upon the following: The question has to be a bit more precise. There is a great difference between the KLA in 1997 and 1998, and these mentioned persons held these particular offices in both years. Please make the question as precise as possible so that the accused, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, would not later abuse an omission made on my part. As I already said, in 1998, the KLA became stronger, but by then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We want to know what Mr. Tomas told you about his level of knowledge in relation to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we talked about the example of Decani. The centre of Decani was razed to the ground by a tank unit of the Army of Yugoslavia, around Easter 1998, under the pretext that they wish to do away with terrorist sniper nests. The special units of the SDB of Serbia knew about these sniper nests. The police could have done away with them without any army participation. Instead of that, the army came in and unselectively destroyed part of Decani, the old part, where Albanians lived, Kosovar Albanians, and this gave rise to ethnic tensions, and the terrorist nests were -- and the sniper nests were not demolished. And the State Security complained that this action was ineffective, and in response it was said that this was ordered from the top, and the shelling of Decani went on for days. I do not know who the military officer in charge of this particular operation was. And as for the -- all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's past the time usually for an adjournment. Are you going to be many minutes more, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think probably about five or ten, but no more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go on, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So no sniper was killed. But generally, what did Mr. Tomas tell you, if anything, about his level of knowledge in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps some sniper was killed, but first and foremost, Mr. Zoran Mijatovic, who was the person in charge, told me that Mr. Milosevic would not allow the State Security Service to operate against the KLA leaders who were abroad, that they do not allow the electronic surveillance of the border, that also he was impeding active measures, as they were called, in terms of Albanian terrorism, also drug trafficking, and also that he refused equipment that was practically offered with a credit, that was entailed for border surveillance. So that he was talking against, but in practice that he was impeding actions aimed against terrorism. Because terrorists were not peasants; it was their leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come back to this page, but paragraph 107 fits together with this. Did you learn anything about what had happened in Likosane and Prekaz? If so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In the village of Likosane, a patrol was killed, a police patrol, which was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You did learn about it. From whom?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomas Bogdan, Mijatovic. And when I use the term "the service," that's who I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what were you told by them about what had happened in Likosane and Prekaz?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The results of the internal investigation conducted by MUP show that the situation was highly suspect, that the police units, our Serb police units in the village of Likosane -- that is to say, they were sent to Likosane, to the terrorist stronghold, which we knew existed, without the necessary equipment, vehicles, logistics, intelligence, and so on and so forth, and it was just as if you had thrown them to their death. After that, our police force, in their quest for the perpetrators, the killers, the Kosovar Albanian terrorists, killed a certain number of people. The Jashari brothers set up barricades in their own house in Donje Prekaz. There were there with their families. And our police force was well aware of the age-old tactics of the Albanian terrorists and Muslims, that in any terrorist [as interpreted], they take a sort of human shield to protect them, both amongst their family members, their friends, and so on. So that is a very ugly thing, but it doesn't mean to say that you can kill them. Now, our police intervened en masse, using force en masse, and along with the Jashari's who were killed, a large number of women, children, and civilians were killed, without any need at all. This gave rise to great concern in professional circles: the police, the army, and the Security Services, because we knew that this would give rise to the Albanians' wish to take their own back and to retaliate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just come back to paragraph 98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you finish that, we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there an identified Albanian called Agim Ceku?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Albanians were identified, several of them. Even when I wanted to learn information about them, I was prevented by people who were loyal to Milosevic in doing so. I mean Agim Ceku, Ramush Haradinaj, Hashim Thaci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you discover - just yes or no - the accused's attitude towards pursuing these people in order to hand them over to this institution, the ICTY? Did you learn about his attitude to those things? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did learn about that, in a very drastic way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, from the leaders of the State Security Service, and then my example, through torture. Because one of the accusations against me and why I was tortured was what did I have to do to meddle into the investigations against the Albanian terrorists together with The Hague Tribunal? So I was beaten for two hours on that particular topic alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may have a few more questions, but it will only be a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 113, page 20. Now, just yes or no to these questions, please. Did you learn anything about the ordering of troops into the Djakovica region in June 1999 or thereabouts? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but before June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From whom did you learn what you did learn?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the Easter of 1998, and it was Bogdan Tomas. Perhaps there was a mistake in the typing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. It's because we're jumping around to tidy up matters that were left incomplete. I'm now moving on to June 1999. During the NATO bombing. There may be some confusion in the typing, you're quite right. But did you at that time, June 1999, learn something about an occasion of ordering troops into the Djakovica area? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but before June. That's the mistake. In June it was almost all over. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From whom did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An officer of the State Security Service, Tomas Bogdan, was down there under direct bombing and was able to see what was going on and what was happening to the troops and how they were being sent off to die under the bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was it that he was able to tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, he said that when they were bombing, it was as if the earth was boiling. That's how strong it was. That it was burning. And that without any need, after the bombing was over, the soldiers had been sent to take control of the fields where the bombing had taken place, and then NATO planes would turn up again and the army would lose their lives again. And the Chernomyrdin agreement was already known, Chernomyrdin-Atisari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just yes or no to this: Did you learn what the troops were supposed to be doing in Djakovica? What was their purpose there? Just yes or no to that.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it from the same Mr. Tomas or from someone else?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, plus subsequent sources afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the troops being there, as related to you by these people?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To expel the Albanian terrorists from the areas in which they could return after the NATO bombing. Then a fresh bombing, fresh Serb victims, fresh expulsions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next question: Yes or no, was Mr. Tomas able to tell you - just yes or no - who had instructed the troops to go there and do that? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he couldn't tell me that. I learnt that in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Without telling us the conclusion, how did you learn it? What was this different way in which you learned it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In discussions with General Perisic later on, preparing the book on the sense of using an army under such circumstances, deploying the army under such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And from that source, as you understood it, who had instructed the troops or ordered the troops to go to Djakovica for those purposes?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, the private chain of command, as far as I was informed. I can't confirm this directly, but it was the private chain of command, going down from Milosevic, via Sainovic, and Pavkovic, without any institutionalisation and conduct in times of war, or even as it was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 131, page 22. Did you learn from any source about - just yes or no to this - who was instrumental in ordering or who ordered the operation in Racak? Just yes or no. Did you learn who ordered that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who informed you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Foreign source.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you name the source?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. I can name the public source.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say the public source. Who was the public source?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The writings of the press, just one paper, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, those are not admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to take that further in those circumstances. All right. That tidies up, I think, the paragraphs that we passed over. I have a couple of concluding question and one other exhibit that we must sort out from yesterday. Let's just deal with a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of detail, when looking at the possible agreement that you've spoken of, had Yugoslavia itself participated in United Nations peacekeeping forces on any other earlier occasions, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the peacekeeping forces, for keeping the peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, do you hold any views about Kosovar Albanians or about Albanians or about their culture? Are you particularly fond of it? What's the position?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal one or the political one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. Your personal one.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because, as a matter of fact, why?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because they do represent a problem for the state and national interests of Serbia, not in the extent to which it is being viewed, but they do nonetheless, especially now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all I want. Can I tidy up the newspaper exhibits that we produced or started to produce yesterday? I needn't go through them. The Chamber will remember that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this from the last witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll remember the problem was that the original newspaper reports had been redacted, and it looked as though they had been redacted to excise the witness's name. And so we had unhelpfully redacted originals with redacted copies. I'm very loath to burden the CLSS with the retranslation of newspaper articles, so what I'm going to propose. If this is acceptable to the Chamber, that we hand in first for yesterday's exhibit the original, which has been underlined with wherever there's a redaction, and -- this is Exhibit 147. And even for those unfamiliar with the Cyrillic script, I think the name of the witness is clearly that which has been redacted. And so that will make sense, if it's necessary to make sense of the English translation. But underlined is "Ratomir Tanic" on several occasions. I think on one occasion his title may have been redacted as well. That's about it. Then there are two other similar newspaper articles, and in this case I've presented them I think as - I hope I have - presented them as a clip of materials where there's the English translation followed by the original newspaper article with underlinings of the redacted passages, and the same for the other. I wonder if they could all become 147. There's no need for them to have a separate number. If that would be acceptable. There are therefore two more parts to 147. And with the leave of the Chamber, if we can save the further translation of the articles that have simply had the names redacted, I think that will save time and money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be helpful to have 147, 1, 2, and 3, so there's no confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Mr. Nice, if you could tell us whether Mr. Tanic dealt with paragraph 108 in page 20 in full after he decided to give evidence publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll ask him once again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll have the article dated 18 September 1996 as 147.2, and then the article dated 31 July 1997 as 147.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question to you, Mr. Tanic, is this, following on from His Honour Judge Kwon's inquiry: In light of your willingness to give evidence publicly, are you willing now to tell us what happened at the meeting in April 1999 with the accused? Just yes or no. No explanation is required.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but with a correction as to the description. The description does not correspond entirely. That's probably my fault in describing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us when it was and what happened.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During April and May, four or five meetings were held. I'll have to take up a little more time, but I will try and be as concise as possible. So during April and May, there were five or six meetings held in Belgrade on the premises of the business club of the Novo Demokracija - the street is Majke Jevrosime Street - between the Italian ambassador, Amerigo Sessov [phoen], and Vuk Draskovic, the vice-president, the vice-premier of the Yugoslav government, the president of my own party, Mr. Dusan Mihajlovic, and myself. The purpose --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, it may be that this background is going to be helpful. Our immediate interest is in what the accused said to you at a face-to-face meeting or a face-to-face encounter, however you describe it. If you can move there very swiftly and then answer His Honour Judge Kwon's or my inquiry with your evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it's about. As we did not have a face-to-face meeting, there was a telephone conference, actually, and I'll take upon myself the responsibility. But I wasn't thinking of going into that, but into some other matters, and perhaps I did not devote attention to that. There was a personal telephone conversation, but not face-to-face, not a face-to-face encounter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was said?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was said was that, quite simply, there would be no ceasefire in the conflict for some time to come, that Serbia and Yugoslavia needed some more civilian victims. This was said upon insistence to bring the war conflict to an end as soon as possible. But nothing -- I don't wish to say anything else about that because there are other traces of that accusation against Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who said that, and who was at the other end of the telephone?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to prove that NATO was a criminal organisation, at the end of the previous paragraph. Communication between Mr. Milosevic and Draskovic; I heard that on the speakerphone. It was a reception, but it was our own reception. Now, may I explain the context of that, if the Tribunal wishes to hear it? Because the context is highly significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. But, Mr. Tanic, we do need to understand precisely what was said. The important part of your -- of this is the conversation. Now, do I understand this all right: There was a telephone conversation between Mr. Draskovic and Mr. Milosevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the open speakerphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you were listening in on the speakerphone and heard what you've described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because it was held in the offices of our own party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned a reception. It might have been a mistranslation. Has that got any relevance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a small reception that we held with the presence of the Italian ambassador, and we used that occasion to -- it was a small reception. I spoke of this superficially earlier on. And the mistake is mine. I wasn't going to talk about it in this way but in a different way. Now we've cleared that up. But the substance of it all is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes all that I need ask this witness at this stage. I will be very grateful if before the close of today's hearing we can have an idea of how long the accused is going to want with this witness. The bulge or whatever it is of witnesses for next week is very difficult to manage and it may be a certain amount of reordering, which I'll be able to give notice properly today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, how long do you anticipate being with this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at any rate, quite a long time, more than Mr. Nice needed in view of the fact that the witness has provided a large bundle of papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. There's no need to go -- no need to go into the detail for the moment, we're just considering the timing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's very helpful. It's probably sufficient for my purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Certainly tomorrow, I would think.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all day tomorrow would be less than Mr. Nice had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're going to begin your cross-examination of this witness. He has given a lot of evidence, evidence relating to you and evidence that will generally be considered of importance to the Chamber. In order to make the best use of your opportunity to cross-examine, I encourage you to keep your cross-examination as focused as possible, confining it to relevant issues, and resisting the temptation to indulge in bickering and perhaps even quarrelling with the witness, and certainly cross-examination should not be used to score points. I thought I should say that at the beginning of your cross-examination of this witness, whose evidence is of importance to you and to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as time goes, I'm going to bear in mind that I have less than 40 minutes left to me today, which means that tomorrow I would spend the whole day and on Monday. I would need tomorrow and the whole day Monday to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is by no means certain. You will certainly have tomorrow. I have just noted that the Prosecution had four and a half hours. If you have the whole of tomorrow, you will have much the same. We will consider what progress is being made and we'll consider the nature of the examination to decide whether the examination will go on beyond tomorrow. On one matter, Mr. Nice, a technicality: Can the witness be here next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No difficulties of any kind. It happens I won't be here, I think, on Tuesday but I can be substituted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll bear that in mind. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. That means that I have at my disposal the first day of the following week. Have we understood each other?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's precisely not what I said. I said you can have tomorrow, and we would then consider whether you can have any time next Tuesday, depending on how you get on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And are you bearing in mind the fact that Mr. Nice started yesterday, started his examination-in-chief Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. yesterday at 20 minutes to 12.00, and that he had a full two hours yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I've considered that. He didn't. He had an hour and a half. But let's go on rather than arguing about the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move on to the cross-examination, then. But I would like to say that the very fact that the first Serb who is testifying here is a false witness, confirms my assertions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a comment. Now, if you have questions, ask them. That will simply lose you time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You claim that you were an associate of mine.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I've never claimed that I was a friend and associate of yours. But due to force and circumstance -- that would be false testimony, if I were to say that I were your friend or associate. But the fact that I was an advisor to the president of one of the three coalition parties over a period of three or four years did bring me into a constant working contact with your policy, and from time to time with you yourself, because you saw that I made a list of very limited circumstances under which we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. We'll come to that, we'll clear that up.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I was very modest in representing all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Associate in the sense that you said that you got from me some guidelines for work, or that I followed or attended some work of yours. That's what you claimed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been asked to wait for the interpretation. I said that on several occasions, as far as the work that I did, first of all on behalf of my party, as a member of the ruling coalition, on several occasions this was confirmed on your part, either directly, but much more frequently indirectly. So I never claim that I was your constant associate or friend, and I depicted this in a very modest manner, my working contacts with you in a very modest way. But the fact remains that we were in the ruling coalition of our three parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into this coalition. You claim that you had direct contacts with me.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you understand Serbian, I assume.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, but for the purposes of the Trial Chamber and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got to remember that this has got to be translated, so leave a gap.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have a question. I don't hear the interpretation, so I don't know when I can go ahead and speak or how long I should wait. That is a problem. It's presenting a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that you were a member of the Novo Demokracija or New Democracy. Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a post in that party, a function of any kind? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, but very briefly, why you think that I, in addition to 700.000 members of my own party, the socialist party, and 150.000 members of the left and other distinguished people in Serbia, why would I need to select you, to issue any tasks to you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't claim that you gave me any tasks. What I said was that you authorised tasks which I was entrusted with and which I performed in keeping with the ones that I was given by the president of my party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So your president, your party president, gave you some tasks to fulfil. Now, did you ever have a meeting with me personally?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday in response to a question from Mr. Nice that you had meetings with me frequently; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not right, because I enumerated the number of times I actually had meetings with you in response to Mr. Nice's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I made a note of that, and that's why I say that he asked you whether your meetings with me were frequent. You said yes. Then he asked you was it more than once, you said yes, and then he asked you how many times, and you said five to seven times. Isn't that right? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and in my opinion, that wasn't frequent. Now, if Mr. Nice thinks it's frequent, well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said five to seven times?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He asked you where. You said two or three times at a reception of the delegation of the Novo Demokracija, New Democracy, and two or three times at other receptions, receptions in the JUL party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was far more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You can be provided with the transcript of what you said. That is what I jotted down and that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then you didn't make a note of it correctly, because I know what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The note which I have was: "Five to seven times, always in a working environment or at receptions. At two to three -- for instance, at two to three annual meetings between the parties, JUL receptions, or state holiday receptions."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So those were those five to seven times; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, just like the distinguished judge, Judge May, said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to interpret this, you never had a personal meeting with me, did you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean eye-to-eye, a tete-a-tete, just you and me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Any meeting.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. Each of these times there was a meeting between you and me, but never a tete-a-tete. There were always other people present. It was always a group of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you're talking about receptions in the New Democracy party, that these receptions were always attended by the media; the press, journalists, TV cameramen and so on. They were always recorded by the media?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I didn't mention a single reception of the New Democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said meetings and receptions that the Novo Demokracija had on an annual basis with me.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, but they weren't receptions by the Novo Demokracija, they were meetings between the Novo Demokracija delegation and you in the building of the presidency of Serbia. There are photographs. This was photographed. I can bring you the photographs tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying. How shall I put this? When the Novo Demokracija turned up, this was a numerous delegation; isn't that right? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, come on.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes yes, sometimes no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At all events, it was always within a delegation. There was always a delegation, and a delegation implies many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've already wasted time, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the receptions in JUL, the Yugoslavia United Left, or state receptions, there were always over a thousand people; the diplomatic corps, representatives of the religious communities, prominent public figures and so on and so forth? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, receptions of this nature, the receptions at which over a thousand people take part, can they be considered to be meetings with me?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described the circumstances very precisely, where there were short brief working meetings with you, Mr. Milosevic, at those receptions, because it was at those receptions, like any other head of state, that you used them to do some business, to hold working talks with some individuals. These were brief encounters, and I mentioned these encounters. I didn't speak of meetings. I was very precise. And when I mentioned your words, I never said that this was a meeting. I just said an encounter in which there was a relevant exchange of opinions. So could you consult the record for that. I don't want it to appear that I was saying something I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're representing everything that wasn't correct, because I didn't have working contacts at those meetings and receptions, and you said that the receptions were fairly rare anyway.
